answer: Yes. Pipe a show into the `display` piped command with the `commands` mode: `<command> | display commands` renders the configuration as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, which is useful for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. The recommended form is `show config | display commands`, storing the result for later usage, which is the documented way to build a CLI script that can restore the system configuration. `show config` displays only non-default configuration (attributes at their default values are skipped) and is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the hierarchy gives the complete system configuration; syntax is `show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]` if you want to limit the scope. `show -r | display commands` also works. Other display modes are list (default), table, csv, keys-table, single-table, only-values, xml, json, xpath and interactive.

Yes. Chain the `begin` and `until` piped commands, which are explicitly documented as usable together to retrieve a sub-set of an output. `begin` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word: `<command> | begin <words>`. `until` displays the output ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word: `<command> | until <words>`. In both, <words> is the line to begin with / end with and may contain spaces if enclosed in quotes; `-h` displays help for the command. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command line, so pipe show into begin and then into until to get the span between the two lines.

Yes, use the `more` piped command, and yes, position matters: multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. Syntax is `<command> | more [-h]`, where <command> is any display command such as tree or show, and -h displays help. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, that is, the terminal size, except for the serial port case where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display pauses; press any key to resume or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space> and <tab>) shows the next page. Example of a filtered listing paged: `tree | include led | more`; also `show -r | more`.

It does not fail: with the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used, it is ignored. Syntax is `<show command> | sort [-h]` or `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`. `sort` with no parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. A list of attributes can be provided as parameters and is used for sorting; <attribute> is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output. To flip the order, use `-i`, which inverts the order and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. Examples: `show card | sort`, `show port | sort port-type`, `show odu | sort -i` (inverted order), and `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date` (sorted by user-group then last-login-date, inverted). `-h` displays help for the command.

Capitalisation does not matter and patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command filters out lines containing the given word or string: `<command> | exclude <filter>`. The <filter> does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed in quotes, for example `show | exclude 'ne oper'`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. `-h` displays help. Examples: `show | exclude ne`, `show led | exclude status`. The complementary commands are `include` and `grep`, which display only the matching lines (grep and include are the same command, and grep additionally supports -a=<n> lines of context after the match, -b=<n> before, and -n for line numbers).

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of a given command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`. More than one word can be provided. Without quotes the words are searched for separately, so `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` highlights 'odu4' and 'oduflex' independently. To mark up a whole phrase, enclose it in quotes so it is searched for as a sentence: <word> may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. You can mix both forms, for example `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` highlights the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the single word 'odu4'. `<command>` is any normal command that generates output, and `-h` displays help for the command.

Yes. The `linenum` piped command adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax is `<command> | linenum`, or `<command> | linenum -h` where -h displays help for the command. <command> is any display command such as tree or show. It takes no other parameters. Example: `show | linenum` displays the output with enumerated lines. As an alternative when you are already filtering, the `grep` piped command supports the `-n` option, which displays line numbers in the result (grep also takes -a=<n> for lines of context after the match and -b=<n> for lines of context before it).
